newsitem.title: USA: Trait "stacking" seen as trend in ag - Novartis.
newsitem.headline: Trait "stacking" seen as trend in ag - Novartis.

text.p: The U.S. seed industry has mastered the technology to make crops pest- and herbicide-resistant, and the next generation of biotech crops will offer farmers seed that has many gene traits "stacked" together.

"That's going to be our next biggest issue--what traits are we going to stack in corn?" said Jack Bernens, director of product development for Novartis Seeds Inc. in Golden Valley, Minn., an affiliate of Swiss-based Novartis Seeds AG.
Currently, Novartis only offers farmers Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) corn seed that is genetically modified to resist the European corn borer and certain brands of herbicides.
But in 1999, Novartis plans to market corn that is engineered to be corn-borer resistant, tolerant to more than one herbicide and bred to produce a higher oil content, Bernens said.

Eventually, seed companies will be able to engineer crops that are pest resistant, disease resistant and have nutritional traits that are desirable for feeding specific types of animals, Bernens said in an interview with Reuters.
"We'll even be trying to tailor-design the grain to whatever type of livestock you're targeting," Bernens said.
Despite Novartis' optimism for increased Bt corn seed sales in 1998, U.S. farmers have shown an initial reluctance to plant Bt corn since its commercial introduction in 1996.
In 1997, it is estimated that only 4.5 million of the nation's approximately 80 million corn acres were planted with Bt corn. In 1998, Novartis sees Bt corn acreage growing to 11 million acres.
The relative high cost of Bt corn rather than U.S. farmers' reluctance to grow genetically-altered crops is most often cited as the reason for low Bt corn acreage.

Resistance to the introduction of genetically-modified organisms in the food chain has been much higher in Europe, where environmental groups have waged high-profile campaigns against food processors and grain buyers.
